impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache, after a jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity. The court found sufficient written description and enablement support, remanding for further proceedings. This decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent holders asserting genus claims covering antibody therapies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of pharmaceutical and biotech companies to obtain and enforce patents claiming genus antibody therapies where the specification discloses one species and references known methods for making others, potentially broadening patent protection for biologics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug developers face broader patent barriers when challenging antibody patents on written-description and enablement grounds, potentially delaying market entry for competing therapies.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights retains sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue third parties for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license—retain sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. The court clarified that the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the license terms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses can retain standing to enforce patents by preserving the right to sue for infringement in their licensing agreements, providing greater flexibility in patent monetization strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from both licensors and licensees, and cannot as easily challenge standing based on the existence of an exclusive license when the licensor retains enforcement rights.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations for a Defend Trade Secrets Act claim had expired before the plaintiff filed suit, where the plaintiff had knowledge of the alleged misappropriation years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL and held that Insulet's DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow was time-barred. The court determined that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. This ruling vacated a jury verdict and damages award in Insulet's favor.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a stronger defense where the accusing party delayed filing beyond the statutory limitations period, even after obtaining a jury verdict.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering misappropriation or risk losing their federal DTSA claims entirely, emphasizing the critical importance of timely filing and diligent monitoring of potential misappropriation.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and its damages model, and whether the jury's breach of contract damages award should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award. The court affirmed the denial of Ford's JMOL on trade secret misappropriation liability, maintaining the finding that Ford misappropriated Versata's vehicle configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from broader latitude in presenting damages theories, and companies whose jury verdicts on contract claims were overturned may see those awards reinstated on appeal.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing internal software after licensing from third parties face sustained trade secret misappropriation liability, and district courts face reversal for overly restrictive exclusion of damages models.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that the plaintiff's asserted trade secrets were protectable trade secrets under California law, and whether the patent invalidity finding should be reversed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding there was insufficient evidence that the four asserted trade secrets were protectable because they were generally known in the field. The court vacated the reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction. It also reversed the patent invalidity JMOL, finding the alleged inventor's contributions were not inventive. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted secrets are truly protectable and not merely generally known information, potentially limiting overbroad trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face greater risk that courts will reverse jury verdicts on trade secret protectability, particularly where the information is arguably well-known in the industry, undermining reliance on jury findings.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement, addressing the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law for multicore processor patents and the viability of doctrine of equivalents theories. The case was remanded for further proceedings. The court's analysis of extraterritoriality has significant implications for technology companies whose accused products involve global manufacturing and design processes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of technology patents may benefit from a broader application of U.S. patent law to products designed or partially manufactured abroad, expanding potential enforcement reach.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global operations face increased patent infringement exposure in the United States even where key processes occur outside U.S. borders.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents related to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communications, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed infringement and damages findings. This case provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology whose claims recite specific technical implementations beyond abstract mathematical concepts may maintain eligibility, and damages awards supported by proper expert testimony are upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry-standard communications technologies face continued patent infringement risk, and the partial vacatur creates uncertainty about eligibility boundaries for constellation-related patents.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices attached to farming equipment are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming-data patents were directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, but vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorneys' fees under § 285. The ruling reinforces that data collection and processing claims in agriculture technology remain vulnerable to eligibility challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in agricultural technology patent cases can successfully challenge data-collection patents as abstract ideas, and may recover attorneys' fees if the case is deemed exceptional on remand.
impacts.negativeImplications: Ag-tech companies seeking patent protection for data-collection and processing systems face heightened § 101 eligibility barriers, limiting the enforceability of such patents.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for summary judgment purposes, and whether the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) applies based on sales of a prior art device without express disclosure of its functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony from a corporate representative is admissible even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and that the on-sale bar does not require the prior art sale to expressly disclose the device's functionality. The ruling has broad implications for patent validity challenges based on prior commercial sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a broader ability to use 30(b)(6) testimony and commercial sales evidence to invalidate patents, even when the prior art product's internal functionality was not publicly disclosed at the time of sale.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidity risk from pre-critical-date sales of products embodying the claimed invention, even where the product's relevant functionality was not publicly known or disclosed.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form that asks a single infringement question covering multiple patents, without identifying which patent is infringed, requires vacatur and a new trial, and whether the jury instruction on § 101 validity was erroneous.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's single question on infringement across four patents was prejudicially flawed because it prevented meaningful appellate review. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on § 101 validity of the '495 patent. This decision reinforces the need for patent-specific verdict forms in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in multi-patent cases can challenge aggregate verdict forms that fail to identify which patents are infringed, potentially obtaining new trials where appellate review is impeded.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk losing jury verdicts if verdict forms do not require patent-by-patent findings, increasing litigation costs through retrials and requiring more careful trial management.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly determined that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents, and whether the domestic industry and validity findings were proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing and selling Apple Watch models infringing Masimo's pulse oximetry patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation. The court found no error in the domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings. This is a landmark decision affecting one of Apple's major product lines.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with established domestic industries can effectively use ITC proceedings to obtain exclusion orders against major technology companies importing infringing products, providing powerful trade remedy protection.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies face significant product import bans when ITC exclusion orders are upheld, potentially forcing product redesigns or removal of key features from products sold in the U.S. market.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a temperature standard in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement and no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents for Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents asserted against Mylan's generic drug ANDA. The court upheld the construction that 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at the field's standard temperature (25°C), a critical distinction given that pH varies with temperature.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from precise claim construction that can defeat infringement allegations when the accused product's properties differ under standardized measurement conditions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection when claim terms involving measurable parameters are construed according to field-standard conditions, potentially enabling generic competition.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) for a refiled declaratory judgment action when it previously missed the deadline to seek a stay in an earlier-filed action involving the same issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of district court proceedings by dismissing the original action and refiling a new one. BioMarin was denied a stay of Ascendis's declaratory judgment action challenging patent infringement in connection with its drug for achondroplasia treatment. This ruling preserves parallel litigation rights for declaratory judgment plaintiffs.
impacts.positiveImplications: Declaratory judgment plaintiffs can maintain parallel district court proceedings alongside ITC investigations when the respondent fails to timely seek a mandatory stay, preventing tactical manipulation of the stay mechanism.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day deadline for seeking a mandatory stay cannot cure the deficiency by having the declaratory judgment plaintiff refile, limiting their ability to consolidate proceedings before the ITC.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination should be vacated where a non-party to the underlying litigation filed IPR petitions on the filing deadline of the actual defendant, and whether the Board adequately addressed certain claim limitations in its obviousness analysis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination for FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings, finding deficiencies in the Board's analysis of certain dependent claim limitations regarding time-delayed reporting of sensor information. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. This case raises concerns about third-party IPR petitions filed in coordination with litigation defendants.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer appellate scrutiny of PTAB obviousness determinations, particularly where the Board's analysis of specific claim limitations is inadequate, potentially preserving valuable patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using IPR as a defense strategy face uncertainty when third-party petitioners file on their behalf, and must ensure the Board's analysis fully addresses all claim limitations to withstand appellate review.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether the settlement's attorneys' fees and incentive awards were appropriate.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees to fund unrelated court technology projects beyond what the E-Government Act authorized. The court upheld attorneys' fees and incentive awards to class representatives. This decision provides significant reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users, including law firms and businesses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses and law firms that are frequent PACER users will receive full or substantial reimbursement of excessive fees charged during the eight-year class period, and the settlement establishes important limits on judicial fee authority.
